# Incident Report: NetSupport RAT Infection

**Evidence:** `2024-11-26-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (26,922 frames, 20.8 MB) + Suricata alert export
**Capture window:** 2024-11-26 04:49:38 UTC to 05:43:58 UTC (approx. 54 minutes)

## Victim Host

| Field | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **10.11.26.183** | Consistent across all alerts/traffic |
| MAC | **d0:57:7b:ce:fc:8b** | ARP |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-B8TQK49** | NBNS, DNS (mDNS registration) |
| Domain/workgroup | NEMOTODES (AD domain `nemotoads.health`, DC `NEMOTODES-DC` at 10.11.26.3) | NBNS, DNS SRV/LDAP lookups |
| Logged-in user | **oboomwald** | Kerberos CNameString (AS-REQ to the DC) |

## Malware Family

**NetSupport RAT** — **signature-confirmed.**

Suricata fired six distinct rules directly naming the family against 10.11.26.183 <-> 194.180.191.64:443 traffic:
- `ETPRO TROJAN NetSupport RAT CnC Activity`
- `ETPRO TROJAN Malicious NetSupport Rat CnC Checkin`
- `ET INFO NetSupport Remote Admin Checkin`
- `ET INFO NetSupport Remote Admin Response`
- `ET POLICY NetSupport GeoLocation Lookup Request`
- `ET POLICY HTTP POST on unusual Port Possibly Hostile` / `ET POLICY HTTP traffic on port 443 (POST)`

Packet-level confirmation: the POST bodies to `/fakeurl.htm` carry NetSupport Manager's plaintext protocol over port 443 (not TLS) — `CMD=POLL / INFO=1 / ACK=1` beacons and `CMD=ENCD / ES=1 / DATA=<binary blob>` command/response frames, matching the RAT's known wire format exactly.

## Delivery Chain

1. Victim resolved and connected to **modandcrackedapk.com** (DNS query at 04:50:14, resolves to **193.42.38.139**), flagged by Suricata as `ET CURRENT_EVENTS ZPHP Domain in DNS Lookup / TLS SNI` — a known fake/cracked-software lure domain pattern.
2. Multiple large TLS sessions to 193.42.38.139:443 immediately followed (~04:50:15–04:50:52), transferring several MB (largest single stream ~5.7 MB) — consistent with the NetSupport RAT installer/payload being pulled down from the lure site. Content is TLS-encrypted; no plaintext payload was recoverable from the capture.
3. Within seconds, the host began beaconing to the actual C2 (194.180.191.64) and performing NetSupport's own GeoIP lookup (`geo.netsupportsoftware.com`) — standard RAT startup behavior.

## Indicators of Compromise

**Command-and-control:**
- `194.180.191.64:443` — primary C2, NetSupport RAT protocol (POST `/fakeurl.htm`), signature-confirmed. Beaconing every ~60 seconds from 04:50:45 UTC through end of capture (05:43:29 UTC).

**Malicious/suspicious domains:**
- `modandcrackedapk.com` → 193.42.38.139 — delivery/lure domain (Suricata ZPHP alert), resolved via DNS and used as TLS SNI
- `geo.netsupportsoftware.com` → 104.26.1.231 — NetSupport RAT's own geolocation check-in (part of malware behavior, not third-party benign traffic)

**Malicious URLs:**
- `http://194.180.191.64/fakeurl.htm` (POST, repeated ~65 times) — C2 checkin/beacon endpoint

**Files observed:**
- No plaintext executable was transferred in cleartext HTTP; the payload delivery over 193.42.38.139 was TLS-encrypted, so no file name or hash could be extracted from that channel.
- HTTP objects successfully exported and hashed are all benign/expected: `connecttest.txt` (Microsoft NCSI), `ProcessMAU.txt` (Adobe update ping), Let's Encrypt OCSP blob, Windows Update CTL files, `loca.asp` (NetSupport geo response). None represent attacker-supplied executables.

**Benign context (not indicators):**
- `10.11.26.3` — legitimate AD domain controller (NEMOTODE-DC), all SMB/LDAP/Kerberos traffic to it is normal domain activity
- `104.117.247.184`, `104.117.247.99`, `23.53.127.*`, `173.222.49.101` (office.net), `20.x.x.x` (Microsoft), `acroipm2.adobe.com`, `www.bing.com`, `www.msn.com`, etc. — standard Windows/Office/Adobe telemetry
- `classicgrand.com`, `confirmsubscription.com`, `css.createsend1.com`, `js.createsend1.com` — Campaign Monitor email-marketing infrastructure, unrelated to the infection

## Summary

User **oboomwald** on **DESKTOP-B8TQK49** (10.11.26.183) visited a fake/cracked-software site at **modandcrackedapk.com** (193.42.38.139), downloaded a payload over TLS, and became infected with **NetSupport RAT**. The malware immediately began beaconing to its C2 at **194.180.191.64:443**, using NetSupport's native protocol tunneled over port 443 to evade casual inspection, and persisted for the remainder of the capture (nearly an hour of continuous check-ins).
